After the wedding Yanzhi kept a habit from her brief life in Shanghai: every morning when she rose she steamed her face with hot water. She had learned it from Miss Lin. Miss Lin did it for her looks, but Yanzhi had found that the smothering heat woke a person faster. She laid a towel over her head, buried her face in the basin, and stayed bent there without stirring until she could feel no more heat on her skin; then she changed to a basin of cool water and washed her face carefully, twice over.

She kept the habit until the day the Japanese soldiers came. That morning a plane appeared over Xietang. It was the first time the townspeople had ever seen one, and its harsh roar terrified them, and thrilled them beyond words too; hands clapped over their ears, they crowded into the street, and the children ran shouting after the plane down the road. The plane made a turn in the sky and, like a bird, let a turd drop. With that turd came a roar, and every pane of glass in the town shattered at the sound.

Yanzhi was steaming her face just then, and the hot water leaping up in the basin scalded a cry out of her, but her cry was swallowed in the huge blast, and even she never heard it. In a few minutes the sky was calm again, as if nothing had happened, and yet the street lay in wild disorder. The terror of the blast sent people scattering, a swarm of flies with their heads struck off. Standing in the street, Yanzhi caught the smell of bean-paste on the air and remembered all at once that she had not had breakfast. Just then Benliang, a clerk of the Tang soy-works, came running headlong through the crowd, his gown fouled with mud and sauce like clotted blood. He saw Yanzhi standing there, hesitated, stopped, and said to her, it's over, it's all over. Yanzhi looked at this clerk of the Tang house dumbstruck. Benliang pointed toward the boiling smoke and the tears came. One blast, he said, and the old master's gone, and the soy-works is gone, and all that's left is a pit. As he spoke and gestured, Benliang saw Baosheng come out of the shop just then and slapped his own thigh: how am I to answer to the young master for this? With that he turned to run, ran two steps, came back, looked at Baosheng, and said, Master Hu, you'll have to make our old master his grave-clothes.
Yanzhi looked toward the soy-works, where the wind was scattering the thick smoke every way, and the light of the day turned all at once dim and low.

Get back inside, don't stand in the street. Baosheng drew her in, then looked back at the empty street and said, I have to go over to the Tang house. The old master of the Tang house had died without a whole bone left to him, and what was laid in the coffin was a suit of grave-clothes Baosheng made with all his care. On the day of the funeral the Japanese captain, only just garrisoned in the town, spared no trouble but came in person at the head of his men to the great Tang house. He not only made three deep bows before the spirit-tablet but put a warrant of appointment into Young Master Tang's hands. At a nod from the captain, the interpreter announced loudly to them all that from this day forward this man was head of the Xietang chamber of commerce and of the peace-preservation association. That said, he leaned again to Young Master Tang's ear and murmured, this is the Imperial Army's recompense to you; know a good turn when you see one, and you'll get by.

Young Master Tang's face was ghastly pale; holding the warrant, he looked blankly at the Japanese captain, and then at the interpreter. Afterward he said to the friends and kin who had come to the funeral, say what you like, the Japanese do observe the courtesies.
You're taking the thief for your father. One of the Tang elders wept the tears of an old man.

It isn't enough for you that my father is dead — you'd have the Tang line end with no heir. That said, Young Master Tang would not look at the elder again; he took up a cup of wine and went from table to table drinking their health. Young Master Tang was soon dead drunk, and the instant before he went down he seized the clerk Benliang and bawled, wine — bring them wine!

No one could hold Young Master Tang back; he vomited and drank, drank and vomited; now he wept, now he laughed, until he pitched headlong to the floor and knew no more. Young Master Tang lay on his bed like a dead man for three days, and it frightened the whole Tang household, high and low. On the fourth day he rose all at once, a changed man; not a trace of grief could be seen on his face — on the contrary, he looked full of spirit. He stood before the hall and said to them all, I must go and take up my post at the chamber of commerce. No one answered him. Young Master Tang set his hat straight, went to the door, turned to look at them again, and saw every eye fixed on his face like flies. Young Master Tang gave a little laugh and spread his hands. The old master's gone, he said; I have to go on living, don't I?

That day, the moment Baosheng was out the door, Young Master Tang came into the tailor shop with a khaki wool uniform. He said it was too big and told Yanzhi to alter it at once. Young Master Tang slapped the uniform and said, once I put on this hide, I'm what you'd call a traitor.
“You're still the Tang family's eldest young master,” Yanzhi said.

No, it should be old master now. So saying, Young Master Tang sat down as he always did and watched Yanzhi make tea, and then all at once he spoke of his dead father — the Japanese had gone that day to bomb the county town but had flown to Xietang instead, taking the Tang soy-works for a Nationalist barracks. He asked Yanzhi, tell me, a soy-works plain and simple — how does it turn into an army camp, seen from up in the sky?
“It was all fate,” Yanzhi said.
Young Master Tang nodded. “Who'd have thought a plane could lose its way up in the sky,” he said.
With that he stood and spread his arms. Yanzhi, startled, asked, “What are you doing?”
“You have to take my measurements, don't you.”
“No need. There's no one in your family whose measurements I don't already know.”
“But I do like having you fuss about me.”
Yanzhi said not a word; she spread the uniform on the worktable and, with a ruler and a cake of tailor's chalk, marked it here and there.
Young Master Tang let his arms drop. “That won't do,” he said.
“Don't worry, I'll pay for it if I ruin it.”
I meant you. Young Master Tang looked into her face and said, in earnest, Yanzhi, a woman as lovely as you is bound to come to grief.
“You're to call me Mrs. Hu, or Shimu.”
Young Master Tang gave a little laugh. “In all honesty,” he said, “haven't you heard what the Japanese have been doing in the county town?”
Doing what? Yanzhi's head came up at once.

Everything, and worst of all they can't bear the sight of a pretty woman; the Japanese are lower than beasts. Young Master Tang said, you'd better rub coal-ash on your face, and change out of the cheongsam, and put on a few ragged jackets.
Yanzhi gave a laugh. “Better save the coal-ash for those two wives of yours to smear on,” she said.
Young Master Tang fixed his eyes on Yanzhi. “I'm speaking in earnest,” he said. “I don't want the Japanese laying a hand on you.”
“And if the Japanese did lay a hand on me,” Yanzhi said, “what would that be to you?”
Young Master Tang was brought up short. “How is it you don't know my heart?” he said.
Why should I know it? Yanzhi shot him a scornful look and, with one cut of the scissors, laid the uniform open.

In truth what worried Yanzhi more was the trade in the shop. People were keen to hoard grain, cloth, and cotton, and simply had nothing made. The streets were cold and deserted, yet the shops still had to open. Young Master Tang not only pasted notices at every street corner but went in person with his men into every shop to give the word: to make a show of Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity, the shops must keep their doors open even with no custom. Young Master Tang put it plainly — it was to keep up a front for the Japanese.

Yanzhi had already cut off her long hair; she wore an old gown of Baosheng's and looked out at the street like a little shop-boy. Her meaning was that if the shop could not close, then it must change its trade. Since everyone was scrambling to buy cotton cloth, they might as well sell cotton cloth — surely they could sell Japanese cotton? But what Baosheng thought of was his master and father-in-law: this shop had been the old man's life's work. Times have changed, Yanzhi said.
“These days,” Baosheng said, “the less you take on, the better.”

We don't steal and we don't rob — what's to be afraid of? Yanzhi said, don't you see prices climbing by the day? Today it's Federal Reserve notes, tomorrow Central Reserve notes, and in the end they're worth less than a sheet of toilet-paper.
Baosheng said no more, and looked at Yanzhi. He found this wife of his, with her hair shorn off, a stranger to him.

When the Mid-Autumn Festival came, Baosheng added two counters in the tailor shop and hung a banner at the door with two characters on it: SILKS AND COTTONS. By custom this called for firecrackers and a feast — a joyful thing, whatever else — but the Japanese strictly forbade the setting off of fireworks and firecrackers. Any sound that might be mistaken for gunfire was forbidden in Xietang. You might say the Taishun tailor shop went into the cotton trade without a sound.
